To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
plasma PRL levels rise following long day photostimulation and that a daily rhythm of PRL secretion may be present in turkey hens.
1) plasma PRL levels rise following long photostimulation; 2) plasma PRL is elevated in birds with incubation behavior; and 3) plasma PRL increases at the onset of the scotoperiod.

1) the daily PRL rhythm is not a reliable indicator of the onset of egg laying in turkeys; 2) PRL is elevated at the onset of egg production; 3) PRL levels do not change during egg production in hens that are good layers; 4) the onset of incubating behavior is associated with a dramatic increase in PRL secretion; 5) PRL levels are low in hens that do not lay eggs or exhibit incubation behavior.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the relationship between PRL and egg production in the turkey.
the effects of photoperiod and the daily cycle of light and darkness on the reproductive system of the turkey.
the regulation of the reproductive cycle in the turkey hen.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the nocturnal PRL surge does not seem to be a necessary event in the onset and maintenance of incubation behavior and egg laying.
a diurnal rhythm in plasma prolactin levels does occur, and that the lowest levels occur at the beginning of the light cycle and the highest levels occur at the end of that cycle.

the PRL levels at lights out and lights on do not change significantly throughout the reproductive cycle and that the increase in PRL at the end of scotophase is not a reliable indicator of the onset of incubatory behavior.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

a daily rhythm of PRL secretion occurs in the turkey hen, but the magnitude of the rhythm is not consistent throughout the reproductive cycle and may not be a critical factor in determining whether a bird exhibits incubation behavior.
PRL is a useful marker for reproductive state in turkeys and that PRL secretion patterns may not be an important factor in the initiation of incubation behavior.
the PRL rhythm is not a major factor in the initiation of incubation behavior.
The main takeaway from our work is that
PRL is not the primary hormone regulating egg laying and nesting in turkey hens.
the PRL levels at lights out and lights on are not different, so the nocturnal rise in PRL levels is not a prerequisite for the onset of incubating behavior.

the timing of PRL measurements may be important in studies of PRL secretion patterns in birds, and that PRL measurements at the end of photophase and scotophase may be useful in studies of Prolactin secretion.
